title: High Voltage Electrician Salary: Award Rates, Casual Loading & Super in 2026-27
description: Find the high voltage electrician salary under the Electrical Award. See base hourly rates, casual loading, super on top, and how to convert to annual pay using 38 hours per week.
salarySummary: For a Grade 7 electrical worker under the Electrical, Electronic and Communications Contracting Award, the minimum hourly rate is $32.13, leading to an annual salary of approximately $63,500 before casual loading and super.

faqs.q: How does casual loading affect a high voltage electrician salary?
faqs.a: Under the Electrical, Electronic and Communications Contracting Award, casual employees receive a 25% loading on top of the ordinary hourly rate. For a Grade 7 high voltage electrician, the base rate of $32.13 becomes $40.16 per hour. This loading compensates for leave entitlements and other benefits that permanent employees receive. The annual equivalent, based on 38 hours per week for 52 weeks, is about $79,400 before super.

faqs.q: Is superannuation included in the high voltage electrician salary figures?
faqs.a: No, superannuation is paid on top of the salary. The super guarantee rate is 12% of ordinary earnings for 2026-27, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830. For a Grade 7 high voltage electrician earning $63,500 base salary, the employer would contribute an additional $7,620 into a super fund. Casual loading does not affect super calculations because super is based on ordinary time earnings.

faqs.q: How do I calculate the annual high voltage electrician salary from an hourly rate?
faqs.a: Multiply the hourly rate by the number of hours worked per week (typically 38 under the award) and then by 52 weeks. For example, $32.13 per hour × 38 hours × 52 weeks = $63,500. If you are casual, add the 25% loading first: $40.16 per hour × 38 × 52 = $79,400. Remember that super is paid on top, and tax is deducted using the 2026-27 resident tax scales.

bodyMarkdown:
## Understanding the High Voltage Electrician Salary Under the Electrical Award

If you are looking for a **high voltage electrician salary**, the starting point is the minimum rates set by the Fair Work Commission in the *Electrical, Electronic and Communications Contracting Award 2020* [MA000025]. This award covers electricians working on high voltage systems, including installation, maintenance, and testing. The rates are updated each year following the Annual Wage Review, and the figures below reflect the 2026-27 financial year.

### Base Hourly Rates for High Voltage Electricians

The award classifies electrical workers from Grade 1 to Grade 10. A high voltage electrician typically falls at **Grade 7** or higher, depending on experience and qualifications. For Grade 7, the minimum weekly rate is $1,221.10 for a full-time employee working 38 ordinary hours per week. This gives an hourly rate of **$32.13**. Higher grades, such as Grade 8 ($33.77 per hour) or Grade 9 ($34.46 per hour), may apply for more specialised high voltage work. These rates are from the Fair Work Ombudsman’s consolidated award.

### Converting Hourly Rates to Annual Salary

The standard formula for annual salary is:

**Hourly rate × hours per week × 52 weeks**

For a Grade 7 high voltage electrician:
- $32.13 × 38 hours × 52 weeks = **$63,500 per year** (before casual loading, allowances, or super)

This assumes you work the same 38 hours every week, with no unpaid overtime, penalty rates, or allowances. The award allows for different work patterns, but 38 hours is the ordinary full-time week. If you are paid fortnightly, your gross pay would be $32.13 × 38 × 2 = **$2,442.20** per fortnight.

### Casual Loading: An Extra 25%

Many high voltage electricians work on a casual basis. Under clause 11.2 of the award, casual employees receive a **25% loading** on top of the ordinary hourly rate. This loading is paid instead of annual leave, personal leave, and other entitlements. For a Grade 7 casual:
- $32.13 × 1.25 = **$40.16 per hour**
- Annual equivalent: $40.16 × 38 × 52 = **$79,400**

You can use [the timesheet](/) to calculate your own figures. Simply enter your base hourly rate (without casual loading) and check the casual loading box to see the total.

### Superannuation Is Paid on Top

Employers must pay super guarantee contributions of **12%** of ordinary time earnings (for 2026-27) on top of your salary. This is not deducted from your pay; it is an additional cost to the employer. For a full-time Grade 7 high voltage electrician earning $63,500, the super contribution would be about **$7,620 per year**, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830. Casual loading does not change the super calculation because super is based on ordinary time earnings, not the loaded rate. See [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging) for more details.

### How This Compares to Other Benchmarks

The **National Minimum Wage** from 1 July 2026 is $26.44 per hour for a full-time adult employee, or $1,004.90 per week. A high voltage electrician’s award rate is well above this minimum. The **ABS Average Weekly Earnings** for full-time adult ordinary time earnings (May 2026) is $2,083.70 per week, which equates to about $108,350 per year. A Grade 7 high voltage electrician’s base salary of $63,500 is below this average, but with casual loading and allowances, it can approach or exceed the average. Check [average pay](/topics/average-pay) for broader comparisons.

### Allowances Can Increase Your Pay

In addition to the base rate, the award includes several all-purpose allowances that are added to your hourly rate for all purposes (overtime, leave, etc.). These include:
- Industry allowance (clause 18.3(a))
- Electrician’s licence allowance (clause 18.3(b))
- Leading hand allowance (clause 18.3(c))
- Tool allowance (clause 18.3(g))

For high voltage work, the **electrician’s licence allowance** is particularly relevant. These allowances are set out in the award and are updated annually. You can find the current rates in the [pay guides](/blog) from the Fair Work Ombudsman.

### Tax on Your High Voltage Electrician Salary

Once you have your gross annual salary, the Australian Taxation Office applies the 2026-27 resident tax rates:
- Nil on the first $18,200
- 15% on income from $18,201 to $45,000
- 30% on income from $45,001 to $135,000
- 37% on income from $135,001 to $190,000
- 45% on income above $190,000

Plus the **Medicare levy** of 2% (using the 2025-26 single reduction thresholds as a guide). For a Grade 7 full-time high voltage electrician earning $63,500, the estimated tax plus Medicare would be around $11,000, leaving take-home pay of about $52,500. Use [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) for a detailed estimate.

### Key Takeaways

- The **high voltage electrician salary** under the award starts at $32.13 per hour (Grade 7) for full-time employees.
- Casual workers receive a 25% loading, bringing the rate to $40.16 per hour.
- Annual salary is calculated as hourly rate × 38 hours × 52 weeks.
- Superannuation of 12% is paid on top of ordinary earnings, not deducted from your pay.
- Allowances and overtime can significantly increase your actual earnings.

For a quick calculation, use [the timesheet](/) to convert your hourly rate to annual, fortnightly, and weekly figures, including casual loading and super.
